source_citation: DWP SSI JSA Statistics March 2016
notes: POPULATION BASE. All 2070 employed by SSI made redundant on 2 Oct 2015. List from Insolvency Service — high accuracy. All DWP figures rounded to nearest 10. Supply chain excluded due to incomplete records. Use 2070 as the correct denominator for all Redcar rates.
comparability_notes: Other sources cite 2200 or 2150 — these include supply chain estimates or all-benefit claimants. Do not mix denominators across rows.

source_citation: DWP SSI JSA Statistics March 2016
notes: 540 of 2070 (25%) still claiming JSA at end of Feb 2016. JSA requires active job search — captures workers not yet employed and not on other benefits. 65% (1350) claimed JSA at least once; of those 40% still on it at 5 months. Remaining 60% (810) ended JSA claim but DWP warns this does NOT mean re-employed — could be ESA / Universal Credit / Income Support / retirement / left UK.
comparability_notes: JSA-only measure. Workers who moved to ESA or UC appear as exited JSA but are not re-employed. Cannot compare directly to German or US studies using different benefit systems.

source_citation: DWP SSI JSA Statistics March 2016
notes: 720 workers (35%) made no JSA claim at all. DWP lists possible reasons: on other benefits (ESA/UC/Income Support); dependent on partner claim; chose to retire; temporarily re-employed by official receiver; left UK. Cannot be read as immediately re-employed. Task Force figure of 500+ claimed NO benefit at all — gap of ~220 likely on ESA or UC.
comparability_notes: Not claiming JSA is not the same as employed. Critical distinction when comparing to Hartz or China shock literature which use different administrative definitions.

source_citation: SSI Task Force One Year On Report Sept 2016
notes: 1990 of 2150 (93%) ended ALL benefit claims by 12 months. Task Force base of 2150 is larger than DWP 2070 because it covers ALL benefits not just JSA. ~160 workers (7%) still on benefits at 12 months — hard-to-place group likely older or health-affected. The 93% exit rate CANNOT be split into the 4 model buckets — retrain / similar / underemployed / exit are all lumped under exited benefits. This is the key data gap for Redcar.
comparability_notes: Most-cited Redcar statistic but least useful for calibration — conflates all positive outcomes. Without DWP microdata (restricted access) there is no clean split into the 4 outcome buckets from public sources.

source_citation: SSI Task Force One Year On Report Sept 2016
notes: 500+ workers (24% of 2070) made no benefit claim of any kind — likely split between early retirees (EXIT) and immediately re-employed workers. Cannot distinguish without further data. Compare to DWP figure of 720 who did not claim JSA — gap of ~220 likely on ESA or UC but not JSA.
comparability_notes: Early retirement and immediate re-employment look identical in this data. Steel sector has strong pensions so early retirement may be more common than in other sectors.

source_citation: SSI Task Force One Year On + Gov.uk 6-month press release
notes: NO CLEAN RETRAIN RATE AVAILABLE. 15510 training courses approved at 12 months; 4300 delivered by 6 months; 12000 applications across all schemes. These are course counts not worker counts — one worker may have taken multiple courses. 2988 workers received job advice (near-universal takeup given base of 2070). 50 former apprentices placed in training or employment — denominator unknown.
comparability_notes: UK training course ranges from a 2-day refresher to a full vocational qualification. German Umschulung in Hartz literature = full requalification of 1-2 years. Not directly comparable without knowing course type and duration.

source_citation: SSI Task Force One Year On Report Sept 2016
notes: SELF-EMPLOYMENT — not in model outcome set. 172 new businesses launched (8% of 2070); 418 received startup advice (20%). 821 new jobs created via SSI Fund; 410 safeguarded. Job creation counts are policy outputs not worker outcomes. Union reps confirmed workers in new jobs face lower pay — consistent with underemployment.
comparability_notes: Self-employment may be elevated in geographically isolated communities where re-employment options are scarce. Flag when comparing to Port Talbot or China shock data.

source_citation: Teesside Live — SSI 10 Years On Sept 2025
notes: 2-year figures: 315 new businesses (vs 172 at 12 months). £9m invested in 23000 training courses within 2 years — still course counts not worker counts so retrain rate still cannot be derived. Government funding cited as £53m here vs £46m (Task Force) / £50m (Teesside Live) / £80m (gov.uk). Discrepancy likely reflects tranched announcements. Use £46m as baseline.
comparability_notes: Funding figure inconsistency (£46m / £50m / £53m / £80m) is a genuine data quality issue — document and flag. Take Task Force own reported £46m as most credible.

source_citation: North East Times Magazine — Routes to Work scheme
notes: Routes to Work pilot (£7.5m): engaged 2800+ people across broader Tees Valley; 488 helped back into employment (17% of those engaged). Covers all Tees Valley long-term unemployed — NOT exclusively SSI workers. Two SSI worker case studies: (1) Ray Milner went Aberdeen bypass 2yr then Hinkley Point 2yr then Balfour Beatty then back to Redcar = SEEK_SIMILAR mobile trajectory. (2) Paul had unemployment with health challenges before Routes to Work = EXIT then re-entry.
comparability_notes: Routes to Work is a regional scheme not SSI-specific. Cannot use 17% as a Redcar-specific re-employment rate.

source_citation: Multiple press sources BBC / History Workshop / Local reporting
notes: 40% surge in area-wide JSA claimants immediately post-closure. Area-level — includes non-SSI workers but SSI was dominant cause. Consistent with DWP data showing claimant count rising 6% to 7% of working-age population. At least 160 former SSI staff remained unemployed at 12-month review per press summary of Task Force report.
comparability_notes: Area-level claimant surge is not directly comparable to individual worker outcomes. Use DWP individual-worker data (25% still on JSA at 5 months) as the primary measure.

source_citation: SSI Task Force / Gov.uk 6-month press release
notes: AGE BREAKDOWN — PARTIAL ONLY. 50%+ of workers seeking work were aged 45+. Employer subsidy age-tiered: £15k for hiring 45+ vs £11k for under 45 — government explicitly recognised older workers as harder to place implying higher exit risk. No outcome rates by age band available from any public source found.
comparability_notes: Age 45+ associated with higher exit probability in most displacement literature. Makes Redcar a harder-than-average episode. Check whether Hartz and China shock age distributions are comparable.

source_citation: Evidently Substack citing Tees Valley CA data
notes: UNDEREMPLOYMENT PROXY — area-level not individual. Area wages fell 0.5% real terms 2015-2017 vs +1.6% rest of North East = 2.1pp gap attributable to closure. Manual jobs fell 10% to 8% of local employment (Dec 2014 to Dec 2016); service sector rose 11% to 12% — occupational downshift consistent with steelworkers taking lower-paid service jobs. One documented worker applied to 50 jobs before finding one. Union confirmed lower pay in new roles.
comparability_notes: Wage data is area-level — cannot isolate SSI workers. However SSI was the dominant employer so effect is largely attributable to closure. Wage scarring is more comparable across episodes than benefit claim data.

source_citation: Evidently Substack citing Tees Valley CA data
notes: RECOVERY TIMELINE. Claimant count rose 6% to 7% post-closure (Sept-Nov 2015) and stayed elevated for ~2 years before returning to baseline Oct 2017. Best calibration point for how long displacement effects persist. Area-level measure covering Redcar and Cleveland not just SSI workers.
comparability_notes: 2-year recovery should be treated as best-case given large government support package. Unsupported closures likely take longer. Compare to Hartz (targeted unemployment duration) and China shock (much longer recovery in affected zones).

source_citation: UK Government Tata Steel/Port Talbot Transition Board + BBC News Jan 2024
subsidy_level: £80m UK Gov Transition Board + £20m Tata Steel; min redundancy £20k per worker (£15k+£5k); training option month 1 full pay then £27k/yr
notes: POPULATION BASE. Tata Steel UK total workforce ~8000; Port Talbot site ~4000. January 2024: announced up to 2800 UK-wide job losses (~2000 at Port Talbot). Of those at risk: ~600 offered alternative roles within Tata = retained. Net displacement: ~2100 direct Tata employees. BF5 closed July 2024; BF4 closed 30 September 2024 — end of 100+ years of primary steelmaking. Electric arc furnace planned to open ~2027-2029 creating ~500 new jobs. Town population ~35000; 2800 jobs = ~10% of total employment. Average Unite member age 36 — significantly younger than Redcar (50%+ aged 45+).
comparability_notes: CRITICAL EPISODE DISTINCTION: 2016 Tata Steel crisis (750 direct Port Talbot redundancies) was a restructuring NOT a full closure — no comparable outcome data exists. This episode covers the 2024 blast furnace closure only. Unlike Redcar (complete overnight closure Oct 2015) this is a phased transition with EAF replacement planned — makes re-employment dynamics different. Government intervention is much larger (£500m EAF grant + £122m Transition Board vs £46m for Redcar).

source_citation: Personnel Today Sept 2024 + UK Government Transition Board
subsidy_level: VR: 2.8 weeks pay/yr of service (max 25 yrs); Compulsory: min £15k + £5k retention = £20k total; Training option: month 1 full salary then £27k/yr months 2-12
notes: REDUNDANCY TERMS. Voluntary redundancy: 2.8 weeks pay per year of service (max 25 years). Compulsory: minimum £20k (£15k + £5k retention). Training package: month 1 full salary; months 2-12 £27k/yr paid by Tata Steel. CRITICAL PERVERSE INCENTIVE: whistleblowers reported that staying in retraining longer than 1 month causes workers to lose the full enhanced redundancy payment — effectively penalising retraining participation. 2000 workers expressed interest in voluntary redundancy. 5000 jobs preserved across Tata UK operations through the deal.
comparability_notes: Redundancy package is larger than Redcar (Redcar workers on standard statutory redundancy terms). However the training-vs-redundancy payment trade-off creates a perverse incentive suppressing retraining uptake. Cannot compare raw retraining rates to Hartz (where no such financial trade-off existed) or to Redcar.

source_citation: UK Government Tata Steel/Port Talbot Transition Board 15th Statement
subsidy_level: £80m UK Gov + £20m Tata Steel Transition Board; £13.5m Employment and Skills Flexible Fund
notes: REEMPLOYMENT INTO NEW JOBS. 332 people directly supported into new employment via Neath Port Talbot Council transition services (332/2100 = 16% of direct Tata job losses). 50+ local employers pledged to support displaced workers. Welding skills academy (UKSE/JES Group) aiming to retrain 300 ex-steelworkers and create 50+ jobs — not yet complete at time of Transition Board statement. Cannot confirm if 332 are former Tata employees exclusively or include supply chain workers — NPT Council transition services cover both groups.
comparability_notes: 332 re-employed is a floor not a ceiling — counts only those accessing formal NPT Council services. Workers who found employment independently are excluded. Cannot compare to Redcar (93% off benefits at 12 months) as measurement definitions differ entirely.

source_citation: Swansea Bay News Apr 2025 + Personnel Today Sept 2024
subsidy_level: Employment and Skills Flexible Fund (part of £13.5m programme)
notes: RETRAINING UPTAKE CRISIS. By February 2025 (5 months post-closure) only 3 ex-employees had accessed the Employment and Skills Flexible Fund retraining scheme per whistleblower reports. Structural barrier: the training option conflicts with the enhanced redundancy payment — workers who stay in training longer than 1 month lose the full enhanced redundancy payout. This is a concrete policy design failure creating a strong financial disincentive against retraining. 3667 training courses and qualifications were funded by the Transition Board across the period — but these are course counts not worker counts (same measurement problem as Redcar). Result: a well-funded retraining scheme with near-zero uptake at 5 months.
comparability_notes: Most critical calibration finding for the model: the retraining option existed and was funded but was financially inaccessible due to payment cliff. This shows that subsidy structure (not just subsidy level) determines outcome_retrain_%. The perverse incentive directly suppresses the retrain bucket in the multinomial logit. Directly relevant to model parameter design.

source_citation: ONS Neath Port Talbot Labour Market + UK Government Transition Board
notes: CLAIMANT COUNT — NO SPIKE OBSERVED. Pre-closure March 2024: 2700 claimants in Neath Port Talbot LA (3.1% of working-age population). UK Government and Transition Board state no spike in local unemployment since September 2024. HOWEVER: Sheffield Hallam University academics argue official figures exclude the hidden unemployed — workers on incapacity-related benefits (PIP/ESA) classed as economically inactive rather than unemployed. This is the same hidden unemployment problem as Redcar. A no-spike finding could mean: (a) workers genuinely re-employed; (b) workers moved to ESA/PIP; (c) workers retired early; (d) workers left the area. Cannot distinguish without DWP microdata. Pre-closure base: 2700 claimants in an LA where 2100+ direct Tata jobs just disappeared — any real spike should be clearly detectable in the data.
comparability_notes: Area-level claimant count is not a worker-level outcome measure. Same denominator and definition problems as Redcar. The Sheffield Hallam hidden unemployment point is especially important for a post-industrial Welsh valley town where long-term health-related inactivity is historically elevated. Do not treat no-spike finding as clean re-employment evidence.

source_citation: Logistics Manager 2024 + UK Government Transition Board
subsidy_level: Supply Chain Transition Fund (grants up to £250k per company)
population_n: ~12500 upstream supply chain jobs at risk; ~2000 employed by ~40 supply chain businesses in active application process
notes: SUPPLY CHAIN INDIRECT DISPLACEMENT. Tata Steel supports ~12500 further jobs in upstream supply chain. 59 supply chain companies received Transition Fund grants by Q4 2024. ~2000 people employed by ~40 supply chain businesses were in active application process by late 2024. Many contractor/supply chain jobs directly dependent on steelmaking processes that already ended (Morfa Coke Ovens + BF5) prior to formal blast furnace closure. Welsh Secretary confirmed supply chain job losses already occurring by July 2024 — weeks before BF4 closure. No individual-level outcome data for supply chain workers available.
comparability_notes: Supply chain displacement is the largest and least-measured component of this episode. Direct Tata losses (2100) may be less than half the total displacement. Supply chain workers are likely lower-skilled with worse re-employment prospects than direct steelworkers. Do not use supply chain figures interchangeably with direct worker data when calibrating the model — they represent a different population.

source_citation: UK Government Start-Up Fund + Transition Board + Dr Calvin Jones Cardiff University
subsidy_level: Start-Up Fund grants up to £50k; Business Growth Fund up to £300k; Business Resilience Fund up to £25k
notes: SELF-EMPLOYMENT AND ECONOMIC IMPACT. 85 new businesses launched using start-up equipment grants (earlier source); Transition Board 15 records 22 new businesses in formal count — gap likely reflects timing and eligibility differences. 43 businesses received growth and resilience grants. For comparison: Redcar had 172 new businesses at 12 months (8% of 2070 workers). Dr Calvin Jones (Cardiff University) estimates £200m/yr earnings loss for Port Talbot town — approximately 15% of gross earnings. Total economic impact estimated at £500m to Welsh economy including direct and indirect losses. Self-employment here may reflect scarcity of alternative employment in a geographically constrained town rather than entrepreneurial preference.
comparability_notes: Business creation rate appears lower than Redcar at equivalent time horizon. Possible explanations: (a) workers aged 36 on average may prefer job-seeking over business creation; (b) larger redundancy payment reduces financial urgency to self-employ; (c) different local economy structure. Economic impact estimates are useful for welfare modelling but cannot be converted to individual outcome bucket rates without further data.

source_citation: Senedd Research / Welsh Parliament — One Year On: How Has the Blast Furnaces Closing Affected Port Talbot? (Gareth Thomas 30/09/2025)
subsidy_level: £80m UK Gov Transition Board: £30m workers/supply chain + £13m business + £29.4m regeneration + £3.3m mental health; Welsh Gov additional PLA and employability support
notes: SENEDD RESEARCH 1-YEAR SUMMARY. Outcomes as of 4 September 2025: 3667 training courses/qualifications funded; 37 supply chain businesses received grants safeguarding ~200 jobs; 22 new firms created + 43 businesses with growth/resilience grants; 332 people supported into new jobs by NPT Council employability team (332/2100 = 16%); ~600 Tata employees offered alternative roles within Tata. ONS: payroll employment in Neath Port Talbot decreased since end of 2023. Annual Population Survey suggests employment rate may have decreased — more reliable data needed. EAF construction started 14 July 2025; expected operational end of 2027 creating ~500 new jobs. Climate Change Committee: important lessons to learn from how the closure was managed — UK and Welsh governments should have developed a proactive transition plan including alternative employment BEFORE blast furnaces closed. This confirms the core calibration insight: advance planning significantly improves outcome_retrain_% and reduces outcome_exit_%.
comparability_notes: Most comprehensive 1-year outcome summary available. Key limitation: 332 re-employed is measured by NPT Council services only — workers who found employment independently are not counted. No clean 4-bucket split available. CCC lesson (advance transition planning needed pre-closure) is analogous to Redcar criticism and China shock finding that displacement outcomes are worse when workers have no advance warning or prior support structures.

source_citation: Public Health Wales Community Survey 2025 + University of Leeds Welsh Steel Research
notes: COMMUNITY WELFARE AND AWARENESS. Public Health Wales survey: 74% of households expect financial pressures over next 6 months; only 32% aware of available financial support schemes; 89% anticipate fewer employment opportunities locally. University of Leeds research on Welsh steel mass redundancies (early 2000s): significant structural barriers to employment transitions + negative impacts on health and housing. Mental health and wellbeing fund of £3.3m established — signals anticipated welfare impacts. Community is rallying round per Public Health Wales but financial stress is widespread.
comparability_notes: The 32% awareness of support schemes is a policy implementation failure directly suppressing outcome_retrain_% — workers cannot access schemes they do not know exist. University of Leeds Welsh steel precedent confirms negative health/housing effects are a predictable sequela of mass steel displacement in Wales specifically. 89% anticipating fewer local opportunities aligns with structural reality: steelworks was ~10% of local employment.

source_citation: Unite Workers' Plan for Port Talbot (Nov 2023) + ONS Regional Wages 2022
geography: Port Talbot / Neath Port Talbot LA
prior_income_band: £32800 median FT wage NPT / est £46k+ Tata workers
notes: PRE-CLOSURE WAGE BASELINE. Tata Steel wages 36% higher than UK average (Tata's own data). Median full-time wage in Neath Port Talbot: £32,800 — second highest in Wales after Cardiff £33,100. Former mining area comparison: Rhondda Cynon Taf £26,900; Merthyr Tydfil £26,700. UK average FT median ~£34,000 (2022) — 36% above implies ~£46,200 for Tata workers specifically. Neath Port Talbot's second-highest-in-Wales wage position is almost entirely attributable to the steelworks — closure removes the wage-premium employer from the local economy. Unite Workers' Plan (pre-closure Nov 2023): UK produces only 6Mt/yr = 60% of domestic need; dependent on imports for 10 of 17 main steel product types. Workers' Plan called for keeping BF4 open until 2034 and building 3Mt EAF by 2027 — rejected.
comparability_notes: The 36% wage premium (est £46k+ Tata workers vs £32,800 NPT median) means any re-employment in the local economy almost certainly involves significant wage loss — underemployment is structurally expected for most workers. This is a larger structural wage gap than Redcar and far larger than the 4-10% re-employment wage penalty under Hartz. For the multinomial logit: prior_income_band is the strongest predictor of underemployment probability — Port Talbot workers should show higher underemployment rates than the German reformed cohort where the wage gap was smaller.

source_citation: Centre for Public Impact — Hartz Employment Reforms in Germany
subsidy_level: ALG II flat rate after 12 months ALG I
notes: CONTEXT ROW. Hartz I-IV implemented Jan 2003 to Jan 2005. Key changes: Hartz I-II eased temp work regulation and created mini-jobs up to €400/month. Hartz III restructured Federal Employment Agency. Hartz IV merged unemployment assistance and social assistance into ALG II flat-rate benefit. ALG I (insurance) duration cut from up to 32 months to max 12 months (18 months for 55+). After ALG I exhaustion workers move to means-tested ALG II ~€400/month. Tightened job search obligations — must accept any reasonable offer. Germany-wide national reform — NOT a single displacement episode. Population base is all German unemployed not a specific displaced cohort.
comparability_notes: CRITICAL: Hartz is a national policy reform affecting all unemployed Germans. Redcar and Port Talbot are single-site displacement episodes. Do not directly compare outcome rates. Use Hartz data as evidence for what happens when benefit/subsidy levels change (policy lever effects) not as a baseline displacement outcome rate.

source_citation: Centre for Public Impact + multiple IZA/IAB sources
notes: UNEMPLOYMENT RATE TRAJECTORY. Pre-reform 2002: ~13.4% including labour scheme participants. 2005 post-reform: ~11%. 2012: ~5.5%. End of 2014: ~5%. Overall reduction ~8-9pp over the decade. Portion attributable to Hartz reforms estimated at ~1.5pp (Odendahl CER 2017) — remainder due to broader economic recovery and wage moderation. ~2.5 million jobs credited to reforms though causality disputed. Long-term unemployment did NOT noticeably decrease per Gustav Horn — benefits of reform accrued mainly to those already with strong employment prospects.
comparability_notes: The 8-9pp unemployment decline conflates Hartz effects with broader economic recovery 2003-2008 and 2009 crisis response. The reform-attributable 1.5pp reduction (Odendahl) is the most credible isolated estimate. Do not use overall decline as a Hartz effect.

source_citation: Price 2020 IZA DP13300 + Kuegler et al. UCL/IMF
outcome_underemployed_%: ~10% wage reduction on re-employment — 80%+ due to lower-paying employer
notes: RE-EMPLOYMENT WAGE EFFECTS. Hartz IV reduced re-employment wages by ~10% (diff-in-diff estimate). Workers accepting jobs after exhausting ALG I earn 4-8% lower wages than absent reform. Over 80% of this wage decline is because workers found re-employment at lower-paying employers — occupational or wage downgrade = underemployment. Earnings of displaced workers tracked continuously employed workers closely until 2003 then diverged sharply in 2005 and remained lower through 2010. Low-skilled workers suffered most.
comparability_notes: Wage scarring of -10% is the cleanest cross-comparable metric with Redcar (-0.5% area wages) and China shock wage penalty data. Note that Hartz effect is partially mechanical — reform pressure forces workers to accept lower-paid work. Underemployment rate in traditional sense (% in below-skill jobs) is not directly measured.

source_citation: Price 2020 IZA DP13300
population_n: all workers affected by benefit duration cut
outcome_share_similar_%: PROXY — faster re-employment but lower job quality
notes: RE-EMPLOYMENT SPEED. Hartz IV increased hazard rate of re-employment — probability of experiencing a 1-year jobless spell reduced by 12.4%. Job-finding rate rose steadily in months before benefit exhaustion and spiked sharply at exhaustion point — workers strategically accepting jobs just before benefits run out. Faster re-employment but lower-quality jobs — workers moved into share_similar or underemployed buckets faster under reform pressure.
comparability_notes: Job-finding spike at benefit exhaustion is strategic behaviour not genuine matching. Key model insight: high subsidy_level slows re-employment; low subsidy_level speeds it but increases underemployment share. This is the core policy lever finding from Hartz.

source_citation: Centre for Public Impact + IAB data
outcome_underemployed_%: high — mini-jobs 7.4m by 2010 / temp workers doubled to 780k
notes: LABOUR MARKET SEGMENTATION / UNDEREMPLOYMENT. Mini-jobs (<=€400/month) held by 7.4 million people by Dec 2010. Temporary contract workers doubled to 780000. Ein-Euro-Jobs workfare scheme: 200000+ in 2005 rising to 320000+ in 2009 then declining to 188000 in 2011. Mini-job growth is the clearest measurable underemployment signal — jobs below standard employment threshold. Reforms increased temporary and marginal employment and raised number of people in insecure jobs and at risk of poverty.
comparability_notes: Mini-job count 7.4m is a stock measure of the post-reform labour market not a flow measure of what displaced workers did. Cannot use as a displacement outcome rate directly. However it indicates a common destination for workers exiting unemployment: low-paid insecure work = underemployed bucket.

source_citation: Petrunyk 2023 Wiley + Hochmuth et al. 2020
subsidy_level: ALG II reduced duration for 50+ (15 months max vs 36 months pre-reform)
outcome_exit_%: EXIT — pension system shift in East Germany
notes: OLDER WORKER EXIT. Benefit duration for 50+ cut from up to 36 months to max 15 months (55+ to 18 months). In East Germany: employment remained constant while unemployment fell — decline in unemployment attributed to workers shifting into pension system = EXIT rather than re-employment. Life satisfaction decreased post-reform more for male unemployed in West Germany driven by income decline. Effect stronger on long-term and involuntarily unemployed. Pattern consistent with older workers pushed out of labour force rather than re-employed.
comparability_notes: Directly relevant for Redcar comparison (50%+ of Redcar workers aged 45+). In both cases older workers are the hard-to-place group most likely to exit. Mechanism differs: UK = early retirement via steel pension; Germany = benefit exhaustion then pension system. Exit via pension route inflates apparent re-employment statistics in both episodes.

source_citation: Jacobi and Kluve 2007 — IZA Discussion Paper 2100
notes: RETRAINING (ALMP) EFFECTS. Pre-Hartz ALMP showed negative mean employment effects — training programmes in early 2000s did NOT improve outcomes on average. Post-Hartz reorganisation of public employment services was mainly successful. Voucher-based training (Bildungsgutschein) improved targeting — workers choose course rather than being assigned. Umschulung (full requalification 1-2 years) shows positive long-run effects but lock-in effect during training depresses short-run employment rates. Caseworker assignment still outperforms pure voucher in some studies.
comparability_notes: ALMP = the German equivalent of retraining subsidies in the model. Negative short-run then positive long-run retraining effects is standard finding — model should account for time horizon. Umschulung (1-2 year full requalification) is not comparable to UK training courses (can be 2-day refreshers). Define retrain carefully before comparing.

source_citation: Schneider and Uhlendorff 2006 — IAB/ZAF — Die Wirkung der Hartz-Reform im Bereich der beruflichen Weiterbildung
age_band: all ages 17-65 (58+ were only 0.35% pre-reform / 1.8% post-reform)
subsidy_level: Bildungsgutschein voucher system (Hartz I/II reform of training)
population_n: ~5600 FbW participants matched against ~2.1 million non-participants; FbW stock: ~300k/yr pre-reform / ~100k/yr post-reform
time_horizon: programme duration + up to 18 months follow-up
outcome_retrain_%: NEGATIVE short-run (lock-in) then +5pp employment probability post-programme — see notes
notes: IAB RETRAINING PAPER — CORE FINDINGS. FbW (Foerderung beruflicher Weiterbildung) participant numbers dropped drastically after reform: ~300000/yr pre-reform to ~100000/yr post-reform (67% cut in participation). Average programme duration cut from ~8 months to ~5 months. Main programme type (berufsbezogene und -uebergreifende Weiterbildung = job-related further training without a formal qualification) covered ~60% of pre-reform and ~70% of post-reform entries. During programme: lock-in effect reduces transition rate into employment by ~64% pre-reform and ~83% post-reform — participants less likely to find work than non-participants while in training. After programme: employment probability increases by ~5 percentage points for participants vs matched non-participants. Pre-reform this positive effect only appears after ~22 months. Post-reform: hazard rate out of unemployment after programme end is +88% vs non-participants pre-reform and +111% post-reform (difference not statistically significant). Key reform finding: shorter programmes did NOT harm the positive programme effect — efficiency improved. The +5pp employment effect comes primarily from reduced withdrawal into non-employment (inactivity) rather than from reducing unemployment per se.
comparability_notes: CRITICAL for model calibration: this is the most precise RETRAIN outcome data available. The +5pp employment probability gain is the causal effect of retraining participation. Negative short-run effect (lock-in during programme: ~8 months pre / ~5 months post) must be modelled as a temporary outcome before the positive effect kicks in. Cannot compare FbW participation rate to UK training course counts — these are full structured programmes of months duration. Population is all German unemployed not a displaced cohort — selection into FbW was restricted to those with high re-employment probability so this is a best-case retraining effect.

source_citation: Klinger / Rothe / Weber 2013 — IAB Kurzbericht 11/2013 — Makrooekonomische Perspektive auf die Hartz-Reformen
outcome_exit_%: 40% reduction in unemployment (>5m to 2.90m) / long-term unemployment -46%
notes: IAB MACROECONOMIC EVALUATION — CORE FINDINGS. Unemployment fell 40% from peak of >5 million (2005) to 2.90 million by 2012 — back to early 1990s levels. Long-term unemployment fell 46% over same period. Matching efficiency improved: +10% after Hartz I+II (significant at 99%); +5% after Hartz III (significant at 99%); Hartz IV showed no additional measurable matching improvement. Beveridge curve shifted inward for first time in decades — permanent structural improvement confirmed. At 300000 vacancies: 4.71m unemployed (Feb 2006) fell to 3.40m (Dec 2009). Effect is structural/permanent not just cyclical — confirmed by decomposition of permanent vs cyclical components. Job finding rate rose significantly 2005-2010. Long-term unemployed benefited MORE from matching improvements than short-term unemployed. NEGATIVE SIDE EFFECTS: Real wage index fell 4% between 2003 and 2007 (Statistisches Bundesamt — gross monthly earnings). New jobs for previously unemployed were often unstable — revolving door effect back to ALG II (Grundsicherung). Atypical employment (temp/fixed-term/mini-jobs) increased significantly. Income inequality increased — disproportionate wage declines for lower wage groups. Hard-core long-term unemployed did not benefit sufficiently from reform.
comparability_notes: Matching efficiency +10/+5% is a structural market-level effect — not a worker-level outcome rate. Real wage decline of 4% (2003-2007 gross monthly earnings) is a different measure from the re-employment wage penalty of 4-10% cited in other papers — the IAB figure covers ALL workers including those who kept their jobs and reflects moderate wage settlements. For displaced worker comparison use the 4-10% re-employment wage penalty from Price/Kuegler. Revolving door effect is the most important finding for model calibration: underemployment/exit is not permanent — workers cycle between employment and ALG II. Hard-core long-term unemployed = the exit bucket — reform did not solve their problem.

source_citation: Autor Dorn Hanson 2013 AER — The China Syndrome + ADH 2021 Brookings Papers on Economic Activity
subsidy_level: TAA (Trade Adjustment Assistance) — up to 2 yrs retraining + extended UI 78 weeks — but reached <10% of displaced workers
population_n: 2-2.4 million manufacturing jobs lost 1999-2011 attributable to China; 36%+ of manufacturing workers in highly exposed CZs
notes: CONTEXT ROW. China share of world manufacturing exports: 2% (1990) → 12% (2007) → 16% (2011) then plateaued ~2010. US manufacturing employment: 18.3m (1991) → 11.4m (2011) = 37.7% decline. China shock explains 55% of manufacturing employment-population ratio decline 2000-2019 (ADH 2021) and ~25% of 1990-2007 aggregate manufacturing employment decline (ADH 2013). Affected industries: apparel / furniture / toys / electronics assembly — concentrated in eastern US Southeast and Midwest. Primary demographic: non-college-educated males. Episode spans ~20 years not a single closure — outcome rates are causal estimates of exposure effects not point-in-time outcomes for a single cohort.
comparability_notes: CRITICAL DISTINCTION: China shock is a diffuse prolonged trade competition shock NOT a single plant closure. Workers did not all lose jobs on the same day — many stayed employed for years in declining industries before eventual displacement. Structurally different from Redcar (overnight closure) and Port Talbot (phased closure). Outcome rates represent differential experience of workers in highly exposed vs less exposed industries over 16+ years. Do not apply these rates directly to a single-plant model without adjusting for the gradual nature of the shock.

source_citation: Autor Dorn Hanson Song 2014 QJE — Trade Adjustment: Worker Level Evidence (SSA admin data 1992-2007)
skill_tier: all (results differ by wage level — see notes)
population_n: SSA admin data — representative sample of US manufacturing workers 1991
notes: EARNINGS LOSSES AND SECTOR REALLOCATION — WORKER LEVEL. 75th vs 25th percentile of trade exposure: -38% cumulative earnings over 16-year period (2SLS; OLS: -20%). Average worker: positive earnings in 14.2 of 16 years = ~1.8 years with zero earnings (~11% of time out of work). Additional 0.5 months receiving SSDI as primary income source for 75th vs 25th percentile. LOW-WAGE workers: stay at initial firm longer → exit during mass layoffs (involuntary) → earnings losses at new jobs only partially offset → high underemployment and exit probability. HIGH-WAGE workers: exit voluntarily before mass layoffs → move to other firms/sectors → modest earnings losses → share_similar or minimal downgrade. Primary growth sectors absorbing displaced workers: retail grocery / physician offices / K-12 education / restaurants — all below manufacturing wages = structural underemployment. Manufacturing wage premium: 43% of non-college manufacturing workers in top third earnings (2000) vs 23% in non-manufacturing — reallocation to services is a wage downgrade for most workers.
comparability_notes: The -38% cumulative earnings loss is NOT an underemployment rate — it is a relative differential between high and low exposure workers over 16 years including both wage loss conditional on employment (underemployment) and periods of non-employment (exit). Cannot directly convert to single bucket rates. Compare to Hartz re-employment wage penalty of 4-10% — China shock losses are far larger and more persistent (16 years vs 1-3 years). Low-wage worker involuntary exit pattern is directly analogous to Redcar older worker displacement.

source_citation: Autor Dorn Hanson 2021 — On the Persistence of the China Shock — Brookings Papers on Economic Activity Fall 2021
age_band: all (out-migration only for foreign-born + native 25-39; older workers primarily exit not migrate)
population_n: 722 US commuting zones; manufacturing employment-population ratio reference
notes: LABOR FORCE EXIT — LONG RUN. 86% of manufacturing job losses absorbed by decrease in overall employment rate — NOT movement into other sectors. Non-manufacturing sectors show NO significant employment absorption (coefficient 0.05 t-value 0.06 for 2001-2019). Manufacturing employment-population ratio impact: -1.79 (2001-2019); total employment-population impact: -1.74 — almost identical confirming near-zero cross-sector reallocation. Effects persist to 2019 — no recovery 9 years after shock plateau. Exit from work is primary means of adjustment. Out-migration: ONLY foreign-born + native 25-39 — older workers do NOT migrate but exit work. Transfers rise modestly: primarily Social Security + Medicare (retirement/aging pathway) not disability specifically. Social consequences: lower marriage rates / increased single parenthood / child poverty / drug and alcohol mortality especially young males. China shock long-run impacts directly comparable to coal industry decline — both show durable non-employment after local industry collapse with no cross-sector reallocation.
comparability_notes: The 86% exit figure is an AREA-LEVEL measure — 86% of net manufacturing job loss in a commuting zone translated into non-employment at the area level. NOT 86% of individual displaced workers permanently exiting. However the finding that non-manufacturing shows zero absorption is the strongest evidence that cross-sector reallocation is minimal. Directly contradicts standard trade model assumption of mobile labour. The coal industry parallel (UK pit closures → durable non-employment) is directly relevant to Redcar and Port Talbot as analogous single-industry community shocks.

source_citation: Equitable Growth review — China trade shock TAA retraining + ADH literature synthesis
subsidy_level: TAA — up to 2 yrs retraining + extended UI 78 weeks + wage subsidy for lower-pay reemployment + relocation allowances
outcome_underemployed_%: PROXY — 70-80% post-training employed but with 10-20% wage losses
notes: TAA RETRAINING UPTAKE AND OUTCOMES. UPTAKE: <75000 workers/year at peak of shock 1999-2011; estimated 2-2.4m jobs lost = less than 10% of displaced workers accessed formal retraining. OUTCOMES: post-training employment rates 70-80% but with 10-20% persistent wage losses. Majority of retrained workers land in underemployed bucket not share_similar — wage losses imply the retraining → similar job pathway is the minority. TAA wage subsidy for workers reemployed at lower pay is a formal admission that underemployment is the expected outcome even for those completing retraining. Annual earnings decline in exposed markets: 0.2-0.5% per unit of import penetration. Labour force participation reduction among non-college-educated males persisted through entire 2010s.
comparability_notes: TAA uptake of <10% is the clearest evidence that formal retraining was not a meaningful adjustment mechanism for the China shock. Compare to Port Talbot (3 workers out of 2100 accessed retraining fund at 5 months) and Hartz FbW (cut from 300k/yr to 100k/yr). In all 3 episodes retraining uptake is low. The wage loss post-training finding directly contradicts the assumption that retrain → share_similar. Most retraining leads to underemployed — consistent with Hartz +5pp employment probability gain but lower wages. TAA is the most explicit retraining mechanism of any episode studied and still produced <10% uptake and predominantly underemployed outcomes.

source_citation: Autor Dorn Hanson Song 2014 QJE — heterogeneity by wage level + ADH 2021 welfare outcomes
population_n: US manufacturing workers 1991 as base — low-wage subset most affected
notes: HETEROGENEITY BY PRIOR WAGE — KEY CALIBRATION FINDING. LOW-WAGE / LOW-TENURE workers: larger earnings losses / exit during mass layoffs (involuntary) / earnings at new jobs partially offset at best / high SSDI uptake / most likely to land in exit or underemployed bucket. HIGH-WAGE / HIGH-TENURE workers: exit voluntarily before mass layoffs / move to comparable employers / modest earnings losses / mostly land in share_similar or retain similar income level. SSDI: workers at 75th vs 25th percentile of trade exposure spend additional 0.5 months receiving SSDI as primary income = proxy for disability-route exit. Social Security + Medicare transfers rise in trade-exposed CZs suggesting ageing-out pathway is significant exit mechanism. Low-wage workers: 2000-2019 two-thirds of employment growth concentrated in bottom earnings tercile suggesting mass downgrade into low-wage services. Drug / alcohol mortality elevated in highly exposed CZs particularly among young males — extreme exit pathway.
comparability_notes: This is the most important calibration finding for the model: prior_income_band is the strongest predictor of outcome bucket. Low-wage workers → exit or underemployed. High-wage workers → share_similar. This pattern is consistent across all 4 episodes: Redcar (older lower-wage workers → exit; younger more mobile → share_similar); Port Talbot (avg age 36 + higher wages → lower exit rate than Redcar); Hartz (low-skilled workers suffered most wage decline). The SSDI/disability route exit is a US-specific mechanism with no direct UK equivalent (UK uses ESA/PIP) but the underlying dynamic — workers with poor re-employment prospects shifting to health-related inactivity — is identical to the Sheffield Hallam hidden unemployment finding for Redcar and Port Talbot.
